title: Does Vendor Image Processing Matter? Learning Echocardiography Display Appearance from Native Beamspace Data

paper.title: Does Vendor Image Processing Matter? Learning Echocardiography Display Appearance from Native Beamspace Data
paper.abstract: Abstract Most echocardiography datasets contain vendor-processed images, but processing is often undocumented and may affect model performance and robustness. To address this, we train a small convolutional neural network to reproduce General Electric display appearance from native beamspace brightness-mode ultrasound, using 8 406 8\,406 recordings from 605 605 unique patients. The beamspace CNN reduces test mean absolute error by 43 % 43\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} over the optimal pointwise brightness map, outperforms an equivalent Cartesian CNN and runs in real time on a CPU. Across the EchoXFlow and CAMUS datasets, unfiltered training followed by filtered evaluation yields the lowest mean Dice for every class, suggesting filtering may be useful as augmentation when evaluation data are filtered or their processing is unknown. Code and pretrained weights: https://github.com/Ahus-AIM/EchoAppearance .
paper.author_block: Elias Stenhede Arian Ranjbar Address: Medical Technology & E-Health, Akershus University Hospital, Norway

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Images shown on a scanner’s screen are processed versions of the native scan lines, and different vendors and presets give different looks. Echocardiography datasets are often shared after vendor-specific image processing, with limited documentation of the operations applied. As these datasets are combined to train deep learning models, such processing may influence downstream performance and robustness across imaging environments. We study distillation of display appearance: native beamspace brightness-mode (B-mode) data in, the display frame of a General Electric (GE) scanner out. We then assess how domain shifts caused by display processing affect segmentation performance across two datasets.

sections.heading: 2 Methods
sections.text: This section describes the three main parts of the article: frame registration, appearance filtering and downstream segmentation evaluation.

sections.heading: 2.1 Registration
sections.text: We use recordings from the EchoXFlow dataset [ 1 ] , acquired during routine clinical examinations at Akershus University Hospital, Norway, with a GE Vivid E95 Ultra Edition and a 4Vc 4D volume phased-array probe. Each recording is exported as beamspace B-mode (polar samples with the sector geometry) and the GE display frame, available as a JPEG of the first frame. Pixel-wise learning needs sub-pixel agreement, so every recording is registered to its display frame: we fit the sector and measure a patch-shift table using locally upsampled Fourier correlation [ 2 ] . A recording is kept when its patch shifts stay below 0.25 px 0.25\text{\,}\mathrm{px} , its fitted sector width is within 0.2 % 0.2\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the geometry. Recordings with colour flow or a doubtful frame match are excluded. Of 13 389 13\,389 eligible B-mode recordings, 8 406 8\,406 pass. Splits are by patient: 5 943 5\,943 / 1 176 1\,176 / 1 287 1\,287 recordings. We scored the test split once, after freezing all models and hyper-parameters on validation.

sections.heading: 2.2 Filtering Network
sections.text: A residual CNN [ 3 ] (32 channels, 6 blocks of 3 × 3 3\text{\times}3 convolutions with Gaussian error linear unit (GELU) activations [ 4 ] ) runs on the native beam frame. A fixed bilinear resampling maps its output onto the display grid, where a small residual head (16 channels, one block) follows; the model has 117k parameters. Initialised as the identity, it starts out as plain scan conversion ( Figure 1 ). The loss is L1 on the display grid over supported pixels, so targets keep their original resolution. We train on 128 px 128\text{\,}\mathrm{px} patches with AdamMuon [ 5 , 6 ] , halve the learning rate at plateaus and keep the best validation checkpoint. The optimal pointwise map assigns each input grey level the median target value over the training recordings (monotone, 256 levels). It is the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) any brightness curve can reach ( Figure 3 ). The Cartesian twin has the same layers and parameters but applies them after scan conversion; only the order of resampling and convolution differs. We train three seeds of each. Metrics are masked MAE, peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity (SSIM [ 7 ] ); intervals use 2 000 2\,000 patient-bootstrap draws. With warmed batches of 32 32 frames (bfloat16), the 117k-parameter beamspace model processes 726 × 274 726\text{\times}274 frames at 22 22 frames per second on an AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 9965WX CPU (16 threads) and 665 665 frames per second on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 graphics processing unit (GPU).

sections.heading: 2.3 Segmentation Network
sections.text: We train separate MViT-v2-S [ 8 ] segmentation models on unfiltered and filtered Cartesian 256 × 256 256\text{\times}256 inputs, evaluating each checkpoint on both domains. The frozen appearance CNN operates in beamspace before scan conversion. Both conditions use identical clips, geometry, normalisation and training settings. EchoXFlow uses five patient-disjoint outer folds and three seeds, covering 1 125 1\,125 clips from 324 324 examinations of 318 318 patients. CAMUS [ 9 ] uses its official 400/50/50 patient train/validation/test split and three seeds per condition. Training stops with validation patience 10 after at least 25 epochs; the best checkpoint is kept. We report spatiotemporal Dice [ 10 ] for the left ventricular (LV) cavity and myocardium, plus the left atrium on CAMUS. Scores are averaged within examinations and over seeds, then equally over EchoXFlow folds.

sections.heading: 3 Results
sections.text: Scan conversion alone has a test MAE of 33.85 33.85 ; the optimal pointwise map reduces it to 5.42 5.42 ( Table 1 ), so most of the difference is a brightness mapping. The beamspace CNN is 43 % 43\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} lower than this map. The pointwise map darkens the input and keeps its spatial structure, while the beamspace CNN also changes the local texture ( Figure 2 , insets). Fitting the pointwise map to each recording separately changes the curve moderately, but still reaches an MAE of 5.0 5.0 on these 50 50 validation recordings, against 5.5 5.5 for the global map and 3.3 3.3 for the beamspace CNN. sections.heading: 4 Limitations and Future Directions
sections.text: Targets are lossy JPEGs of one frame per recording from one scanner (GE Vivid E95 Ultra Edition) and probe (4Vc). The model reproduces observed appearance. Future work could evaluate appearance filtering in other echocardiographic tasks, including image-based probe guidance [ 11 ] and the training of foundation models [ 12 ] .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusions
sections.text: A small beamspace CNN approximates GE display appearance efficiently and improves fidelity over pointwise mapping and a matched Cartesian CNN. Segmentation degrades when preprocessing changes between training and evaluation, while matched training yields small differences. More broadly, this work highlights the need for considering postprocessing settings before feeding data into deep learning systems, and provides a CNN for approximating one kind of vendor-specific postprocessing.
